pieces.title: A Tale of Five Mangoes
pieces.body:
He shouldn’t be here
                                                  He is a good Christian boy
                                                           His friends laugh
“It’s no devil's ploy”
                                                So he looks at the mangoes
                                                    The forbidden fruits
                                                           Up Kojo goes
                                                    With his loyal druids
                                               He steadies his wheelchair
                                                    Their getaway vehicle
                                        There's a giggle from up the tree
                                                   Why are they so free?
                                      “Hurry!”
                                             He whisper-shouts
                                                     Mangoes come raining down
                                             Little Kwame wears a frown
                                      But does his best to catch them all
                                               They should be more careful
                                                                 Lest they              fall
                                                      He has five now
                                             And still wears the frown
                                                Many surround him
                                   They'll get them when they return
                                 There's a stir inside and everyone's still
                Who else could they expect but the one who pays the bill?
                                                         The creaking door sends everyone running
Left on the floor is our poor little Kwame

pieces.title: The Borrowed Suit
pieces.subtitle: an opening
pieces.body:
Kweku owned exactly one good suit, and it belonged to his cousin. He had borrowed it for a funeral three years ago and the funeral, in a sense, had never quite ended. There was always another one to attend, another reason the suit could not yet go home.

His cousin had stopped asking. This, Kweku decided, was a form of generosity, and he intended to honour it for as long as the lining held.

pieces.title: On Laughing in the Lecture Hall
pieces.subtitle: why comedy belongs in serious work
pieces.body:
We are taught to mistrust laughter in serious rooms, as though a joke were a leak in the argument. Yet the oldest teachers in this part of the world knew better. The storyteller by the fire did not choose between instruction and delight. She smuggled the lesson inside the laugh, and the laugh carried it further than solemnity ever could.

A classroom that never laughs is not more rigorous. It is only quieter about what it has failed to make memorable.

pieces.title: What We Mean by Postcolonial
pieces.subtitle: a word, unpacked
pieces.body:
The word arrives heavy with seminars, but the idea underneath it is plain enough to share at a table. It asks a simple question. After the soldiers and the flags have gone, who still owns the story? Whose language do we dream in, whose history fills the schoolbook, whose name is on the building?

Scholarship dresses this question in long clothes. Our task, when we write for a wider room, is to let it walk in barefoot and still be taken seriously.
